title: Acids, Bases & Salts

notes.heading: 1. Brønsted-Lowry / Lewis Theories, Kw & Dilute-Acid pH
notes.proseLatex: Brønsted-Lowry acids donate $\text{H}^+$ and bases accept $\text{H}^+$ (conjugate pairs differ by exactly one $\text{H}^+$, e.g., $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^- / \text{HPO}_4^{2-}$); Lewis acids accept an electron pair ($\text{BF}_3, \text{AlCl}_3, \text{Ag}^+$) and Lewis bases donate one ($\text{NH}_3, \text{OH}^-$). At $25^\circ\text{C}$, $K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-14}$, so $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14$ where $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]$. For weak monoprotic acid ($K_a$), $[\text{H}^+] \approx \sqrt{K_a C}$.

keyFormulas.label: Water Ionic Product, pH & Ostwald Weak-Acid Formula
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Calculate pH of strong, weak, and ultra-dilute (10^-8 M) acid/base solutions.

examples.problemLatex: Find the pH of $10^{-8}\text{ M}$ aqueous $\text{HCl}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$ ($\log_{10} 1.1 \approx 0.04$).
stepsLatex: Do NOT write $\text{pH} = 8$ (an acid at $25^\circ\text{C}$ cannot be basic!). Include water autoionization: $[\text{H}^+] \approx 10^{-8} + 10^{-7} = 1.1\times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$ (more precisely $1.05\times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$).

notes.heading: 2. Buffers (Henderson-Hasselbalch), Salt Hydrolysis & Indicators
notes.proseLatex: An acidic buffer (weak acid + conjugate salt, e.g., $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) resists pH drift via $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log_{10}\!\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]}$. Salt of weak acid + strong base hydrolyzes to give BASIC solution ($\text{pH} = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_a + \log C)$), whereas strong acid + weak base gives ACIDIC solution ($\text{pH} = 7 - \frac{1}{2}(\text{p}K_b + \log C)$). Phenolphthalein ($\text{pH } 8.3\text{--}10$) suits weak-acid vs strong-base titrations; methyl orange ($\text{pH } 3.1\text{--}4.4$) suits strong-acid vs weak-base.

keyFormulas.label: Henderson-Hasselbalch Buffer & Salt Hydrolysis
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compute buffer pH, maximum buffer capacity (pH = pKa), and salt-solution pH.

notes.heading: 3. Molarity, Normality, n-Factor & Equivalence Law
notes.proseLatex: Molarity $M = n_{\text{mol}}/V(\text{L})$ depends on temperature, whereas molality $m = n_{\text{mol}}/W_{\text{solvent}}(\text{kg})$ is temperature-independent! Normality $N = n_f \times M$ uses valence factor $n_f$ (basicity for acids: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\to 2$, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\to 3$, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3\to 2$, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2\to 1$!). At complete neutralization, gram equivalents match: $N_1 V_1 = N_2 V_2$.

keyFormulas.label: Normality-Molarity & Neutralization Equivalence
keyFormulas.latex: $N = n_f \cdot M,\qquad E = \frac{\text{Molar mass}}{n_f},\qquad N_1 V_1 = N_2 V_2$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Convert molarity to normality (especially oxoacids of phosphorus) and solve titrations.

examples.problemLatex: What volume of $0.2\text{ M }\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ completely neutralizes $40\text{ mL}$ of $0.5\text{ M }\text{NaOH}$?
stepsLatex: Normality of dibasic $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: $N_1 = 2 \times 0.2 = 0.4\text{ N}$; for $\text{NaOH}$: $N_2 = 1 \times 0.5 = 0.5\text{ N}$.
Equate milliequivalents $N_1 V_1 = N_2 V_2 \implies 0.4\,V_1 = 0.5 \times 40 \implies V_1 = 50\text{ mL}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Three Languages for Acid & Base
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: The definitions widen in steps, and each retains the earlier one. Arrhenius (water-bound): an acid raises $[\text{H}^+]$, a base raises $[\text{OH}^-]$. Brønsted-Lowry (proton transfer): an acid DONATES $\text{H}^+$, a base ACCEPTS it, and every reaction pairs two conjugate couples that differ by exactly one $\text{H}^+$ — e.g. $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3/\text{HCO}_3^-$ and $\text{HCO}_3^-/\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, which makes $\text{HCO}_3^-$ amphiprotic (donor AND acceptor). The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. Lewis (widest): an acid accepts an electron pair, a base donates one — so $\text{BF}_3$ is a Lewis acid with no proton at all, $\text{NH}_3$ a Lewis base. Exam shortcut: every Brønsted acid-base reaction is also a Lewis acid-base reaction, but not every Lewis acid contains hydrogen. Micro-check: the conjugate BASE of $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ is $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ (remove one $\text{H}^+$, charge drops by one).

conceptPrimer.heading: Water's Autopilot: $K_w$, pH & pOH
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Water ionizes itself in a tug-of-war: $\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-$ with $K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-14}$ at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$, giving $pH + pOH = 14$ and $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-7}$ for pure water. The scale is logarithmic: one pH unit is a ten-fold jump in $[\text{H}^+]$, so pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4, not one. Temperature bends the ruler — autoionization is endothermic, so hot water has larger $K_w$ and a neutral pH below 7 (still neutral: neutrality means $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]$, not pH 7). And $K_w$ is the universal peace treaty: even in acid solution $[\text{OH}^-] = K_w/[\text{H}^+]$ never vanishes. Micro-check: $0.01\text{ M NaOH}$ gives $pOH = 2$, so $pH = 12$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Strong vs Weak: The Ionization Ladder
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Strong electrolytes ($\text{HCl}$, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, $\text{HNO}_3$, $\text{NaOH}$) ionize completely — $[\text{H}^+]$ comes straight from concentration times basicity. Weak electrolytes ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, $\text{NH}_3$, carbonic acid) only partially ionize, and the fraction is governed by $K_a$: for $\text{HA}$ with initial concentration $C$, Ostwald's law says $K_a = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha} \approx C\alpha^2$ when $\alpha \ll 1$, so $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$ and $[\text{H}^+] \approx \sqrt{K_a C}$. Dilution is the great equalizer: diluting RAISES $\alpha$ while $K_a$ itself never moves (constants change only with temperature). Never use the strong-acid shortcut on a weak acid — Micro-check: $0.1\text{ M acetic acid}$, $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ gives $[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.34 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}$, $pH \approx 2.87$ — not pH 1.

conceptPrimer.heading: Common-Ion Effect & Buffers
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Adding an ion a weak electrolyte already produces pushes its ionization backward (Le Chatelier applied to ions) — the common-ion effect. A buffer exploits exactly that: a weak partner plus its salt (e.g. $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$, or $\text{NH}_4\text{OH} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$) resists pH drift because the salt's flood of common ions pins the ionization near zero change. Henderson-Hasselbalch turns it into arithmetic: $pH = pK_a + \log_{10}\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$. Buffer capacity peaks at the 1:1 recipe ($pH = pK_a$) and works best when the target pH is within $\pm 1$ of $pK_a$; a basic buffer needs $pOH = pK_b + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{base}]}$. Micro-check: with $[\text{salt}]/[\text{acid}] = 10$, $pH = pK_a + 1$; with ratio $0.1$, $pH = pK_a - 1$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Salts That Shift pH: Hydrolysis & Indicators
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A salt inherits its pH from its weak parent: strong acid + strong base ($\text{NaCl}$) hydrolyzes not — neutral; weak acid + strong base ($\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) has a hydrolyzing anion with $K_h = K_w/K_a$, giving basic solutions ($pH = \frac{1}{2}(pK_w + pK_a + \log C)$); weak base + strong acid ($\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$) has a hydrolyzing cation with $K_h = K_w/K_b$, giving acidic solutions ($pH = \frac{1}{2}(pK_w - pK_b + \log C)$); weak-weak salts split by whichever constant is bigger. Indicators are themselves weak acids whose ionized and unionized forms have different colours, so they flip over roughly $pK_{\text{In}} \pm 1$ — pick the indicator whose range covers the equivalence point: phenolphthalein ($8.3\text{–}10$) for weak-acid-strong-base titrations, methyl orange ($3.1\text{–}4.4$) for strong-acid-weak-base. Micro-check: $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ solution turns methyl orange red — acidic, exactly as its weak-base parent predicts.

conceptPrimer.heading: $K_{sp}$, $Q$ and the Endpoint Arithmetic
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: For a sparingly soluble salt $A_xB_y \rightleftharpoons xA^{y+} + yB^{x-}$, the solubility product is $K_{sp} = [A^{y+}]^x[B^{x-}]^y$ written with saturated-solution concentrations — stoichiometry matters: $AB$ gives $K_{sp} = S^2$, $AB_2$ gives $K_{sp} = 4S^3$. The working decision compares the ionic product $Q$ (same expression, whatever concentrations actually exist) with $K_{sp}$: $Q < K_{sp}$ unsaturated (more dissolves), $Q = K_{sp}$ saturated edge, $Q > K_{sp}$ precipitate forms until $Q$ sinks back. A common ion always lowers solubility — $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves far worse in $\text{AgNO}_3$ than in water. Titration arithmetic rides on equivalents: normality $N = n_f \times M$ captures the reactive capacity per litre, and at any equivalence point $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$. Micro-check: $K_{sp}(\text{AgCl}) = 1.8 \times 10^{-10}$ gives $S = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.34 \times 10^{-5}\text{ M}$ in pure water.

keyDefinitions.definition: An acid increases $[\text{H}^+]$ and a base increases $[\text{OH}^-]$ in aqueous solution — the water-bound, narrowest definition.
An acid donates a proton, a base accepts one; every such reaction exchanges $\text{H}^+$ between two couples.
Two species differing by exactly one transferable $\text{H}^+$ (e.g. $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}/\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$); strong acid ↔ weak conjugate base.
A species that can both donate and accept a proton — e.g. $\text{HCO}_3^-$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$.
An electron-pair ACCEPTOR (acid) and electron-pair DONOR (base) — the widest definition; covers species with no hydrogen at all ($\text{BF}_3$).
The fraction of dissolved electrolyte actually split into ions; rises with dilution for weak electrolytes, equals 1 for strong ones.
A weak partner + its salt mixture that resists pH change on small dilution or small acid/base addition; capacity is maximal at equal partner concentrations.
The backward shift of a weak electrolyte's ionization (or a salt's solubility) caused by adding a soluble source of an ion it already produces.
The reaction of a salt's ion with water that shifts pH — anion hydrolysis makes basic solutions, cation hydrolysis makes acidic ones; salts of two strong parents do not hydrolyze.
$K_{sp}$: the ion-concentration product of a saturated solution (a temperature constant). $Q$: the same product from any actual concentrations; $Q > K_{sp}$ means precipitation.
Normality = molarity × $n_f$, where $n_f$ is the reactive units per formula (H⁺ delivered, OH⁻ delivered, or electrons transferred) in the reaction actually happening.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The pH of a $10^{-3}\text{ M}$ aqueous $\text{HCl}$ solution at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $\text{HCl}$ is a strong monobasic acid: $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-3}\text{ M}$ directly, so $pH = -\log(10^{-3}) = 3$.
A conjugate base = the species after donating one $\text{H}^+$: remove one H and the charge falls by one, $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^- \to \text{HPO}_4^{2-}$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: When a weak acid solution is diluted, which combination is correct?
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Ostwald: $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$ — dilution lowers $C$, raising $\alpha$, but equilibrium constants change only with temperature, never with dilution.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: For an acidic buffer, $\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} = 10$. The pH exceeds $pK_a$ by:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Henderson-Hasselbalch: $pH = pK_a + \log_{10}(10) = pK_a + 1$. Ratio $0.1$ would give $-1$; ratio $1$ gives $0$.

options.latex: neutral, because both parents are strong

mcqSelfTest.explanation: $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ = weak base ($\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$) + strong acid ($\text{HCl}$): the cation hydrolyzes ($K_h = K_w/K_b$), releasing $\text{H}^+$ — acidic.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The solubility of $\text{AgCl}$ in $0.1\text{ M }\text{AgNO}_3$ compared with pure water is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Common-ion effect: the added $\text{Ag}^+$ forces $K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+][\text{Cl}^-]$ to be met with a much smaller $[\text{Cl}^-]$ — solubility drops (it is suppressed, not zero).

memoryHooks: The $K_w$ trio at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$: $10^{-14}$, pH + pOH = 14, neutral = 7 — all three move together when temperature moves.
pH is a log ruler: one unit = ten-fold change in $[\text{H}^+]$.
Conjugate pairs differ by exactly one $\text{H}^+$ (and one unit of charge).
Lower $pK_a$ = stronger acid; $K_a \cdot K_b = K_w$ finds the partner constant.
Dilution raises $\alpha$; constants never follow dilution.
1:1 buffer sits exactly at $pH = pK_a$; stay within $pK_a \pm 1$ for capacity.
A salt follows its WEAK parent: weak-acid parent → basic salt, weak-base parent → acidic salt.
$Q > K_{sp}$ means precipitate now; compare only after mixing/dilution.
$N = n_f \times M$, and endpoints obey $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$.
Indicator range hugs $pK_{\text{In}} \pm 1$ — match it to the endpoint, not the start.
Bridge only: equilibrium constants ($K$, $K_a$, $K_{sp}$) change with temperature alone — the full $K_c/K_p$ machinery lives in Unit C05.
commonMistakes: Using the strong-acid shortcut on weak acids: for $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, $[\text{H}^+] \neq C$ — go through $K_a$ and $\alpha$ (Ostwald) or you will grossly overstate $[\text{H}^+]$.
Confusing the degree of ionization $\alpha$ with the constant $K_a$: dilution raises $\alpha$ but leaves $K_a$ fixed at a given temperature.
Plugging INITIAL concentrations into $K_a$/$K_b$ — only the equilibrium row of the ICE table may enter a constant.
Treating pH 7 as neutral at every temperature — neutrality is $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]$; hot water is neutral below pH 7.
Comparing $Q$ with $K_{sp}$ using pre-mixing concentrations — dilute first (volumes add), then compute $Q$.
Counting every H as reactive: $n_f$ comes from the reaction actually occurring (e.g. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3$ is dibasic, not tribasic) — overcounting inflates normality.
Pairing the indicator to the analyte instead of the equivalence point: weak-acid-strong-base endpoints are basic (phenolphthalein), strong-acid-weak-base endpoints are acidic (methyl orange).
Flipping the Henderson ratio: $\log\frac{[\text{acid}]}{[\text{salt}]}$ instead of $\log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$ moves pH the wrong way.
Interchanging molarity and normality inside $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$ — the law is true for normalities (reactive units), not for molarities of different $n_f$.
examChecklist: Classify first: strong or weak electrolyte? It decides whether $[\text{H}^+]$ comes from $C$ directly or from $\sqrt{K_aC}$.
Identify conjugate pairs by removing/adding exactly one $\text{H}^+$ and one unit of charge.
At $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ quote the trio: $K_w = 10^{-14}$, pH + pOH = 14, neutral pH 7 — with the temperature caveat ready.
Weak acid: write $K_a = C\alpha^2/(1-\alpha)$, then simplify to $\sqrt{K_aC}$ only when $\alpha \ll 1$ is justified.
Buffer questions: name the weak partner + its salt, then Henderson-Hasselbalch with the salt-to-acid ratio.
Salt pH: identify both parents; the weak parent decides the direction (basic or acidic).
$K_{sp}$: write the stoichiometric expression ($S^2$, $4S^3$…) BEFORE substituting numbers.
Mixing problems: compute diluted concentrations first, then compare $Q$ with $K_{sp}$.
Titration endpoints: convert to normality ($N = n_fM$) and apply $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$.
Indicator choice: cover the equivalence-point pH, not the initial pH.
Any temperature outside $25^{\circ}\text{C}$: re-anchor $K_w$ before using the 14 bridge.
